name: Chloe Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study computer science. My week is lectures Monday to Thursday, a software project in a team of four, and choir practice on Wednesday evenings at my parish church. I have my own room in a student flat, paid for by my parents. They own three hardware shops, and I go home most Saturdays to help with the till and the stock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love building things people can use, and I'm already making a stock-checking tool for my parents' shops. What wears me out is that I never switch off, because I'm always thinking of the next feature. I got in with average grades, but I work harder than most people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because steady is good for business. I'd tell my friends to keep building, hype or not. Online I'd post about the stock tool, not about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel confident. My skills are useful with or without a revolution, and the shops will carry on. I'd have a safe route through my parents' business and a path through a software job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building. I'd finish the stock tool by spring and put it in the first shop, then the other two. I'd apply for a summer software job, ideally at a company that sells to small shops, so I learn what customers like me need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and busy, which is how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Would you still, in a plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. I'd still use AI every day, because it saves me hours, and I'd rather spend those hours building the next thing. It's just a good tool, whether it's hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your parents' shops change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd carry on selling paint, tools and timber. People still fix their houses. My brother Mateo manages the busiest shop, and my parents plan to keep all three in the family.

say: I'd say good, because **steady** is good for business.
I'd post about my **stock tool**, not about AI.
think: My skills are useful with or without a **revolution**.
I have a safe route through my parents' **shops** and a software job.
do: Finish the **stock tool** by spring and roll it out to all three shops.
Apply for a summer job at a firm selling software to **small shops**.
feel: **Calm** and busy, as I like it.
S0.quote: I'd still use AI every day, because it saves me hours, and I'd rather spend those hours building the next thing.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **daily tool** and a time-saver.
Family business gives her a testing ground and a fallback.
Ambitious without being anxious in the plateau.

steps.text: Finish the stock tool and install it in the first shop
Apply for a summer job at a firm selling software to small shops
Use AI daily to speed up coding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity if you're ready. I'd tell friends to get on with learning rather than complaining. Online I'd share what works for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my fellow students in basic coding jobs will struggle, because that's what AI does best. But a student who knows how to use it and understands a real business will do well. I'd put myself in that second group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd speed up. I'd use AI to build features faster, learn how small shops buy and sell, and sell my tool to two shops outside the family. That would give me real customers and a real product. I'd also keep my grades decent, because employers still look at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, and a bit tense. I like the feeling that things are moving, but I don't want to fall behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the shops change if software took over thinking tasks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shops' ordering, price checks and customer questions could be done by software. It would make small shops competitive with the big chains, which helps my family. We'd need fewer office staff, though, and some of them are old friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly stay out of the way, and keep the rules simple. I'd like government to help people learn skills and then get out of the way of people who want to work. I don't like handouts as the main answer.

I'd tell friends to get on with **learning** rather than complaining.
think: Students in **basic coding** jobs will struggle because that's what AI does best.
A student who knows AI and a **real business** will do well.
do: Use AI to build features faster and sell my tool to **two outside shops**.
Keep **grades** decent, since employers still look at them.
feel: **Excited** and a bit tense, wanting not to fall behind.
S1.quote: I'd like government to help people learn skills and then get out of the way of people who want to work.
fieldNote: She wants **real customers** to prove her tool beyond the family.
Sees AI as a leveller for small shops against big chains.
Concerned about old friends in her family's office.

steps.text: Sell the stock tool to two shops outside the family
Use AI to build new features weekly
Add ordering and price checks to the shops' system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest change since the internet, and most people aren't ready. I'd tell friends to build something, anything, and not just wait. Online I'd share ways to use AI to run a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm nervous. If AI does all thinking work by 2028, software development changes completely, and I'd be graduating into that. The shops are hands-on, so they'd last longer, but even the office side would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd throw myself into the shops' system. I'd get my tool running in all three shops by the summer and make my parents see it as a real asset. I'd talk to an uncle who runs a distribution business about selling it to him. If AI does coding, I'd rather own the business using it than compete for a coding job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I pray, I make a plan and I go to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first month, with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a family meeting. If the thinking work goes to AI by 2028, I'd rather own a business that uses it than apply for a job doing what it does. I'd ask them to let me take on more of the shops' systems and decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say work hard and trust God, and my mum would ask about money. They'd both be worried and both be supportive. They'd keep paying while I did this, I'm certain.

I'd tell friends to build **something** and not wait.
think: If AI does all thinking work by 2028, **software** development changes completely.
The shops are hands-on, so they last longer, but the **office side** would change too.
do: Get my tool running in all three **shops** by summer.
Talk to my uncle in **distribution** about selling it to him.
feel: **Anxious**, but not frozen: I pray, make a plan and go to work.
S2.quote: If the thinking work goes to AI by 2028, I'd rather own a business that uses it than apply for a job doing what it does.
fieldNote: She chooses **ownership** over employment, which fits her traditional, free-market views.
Faith and family structure her response to fear.
Expects parents to keep paying while she builds.

steps.text: Get the stock tool running in all three shops by summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's enough time to be ready, if you start now. I'd tell friends to stop waiting for schools to teach them. Online I'd share how I'm building the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel good but tense. I'd graduate in 2029 with two years to build a business before AGI. Robots reach the shops around 2034, so I'd plan for that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree because it opens doors. I'd spend my holidays building the tool into a product and take it to ten shops. I'd also work with my brother Mateo on how the shops could use robots for stock and delivery, years before they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but pleased with the time. Five years lets me finish my degree, build a real product and still have a plan for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you finish your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. A degree is a base, and with five years it's affordable. It shows I can finish things, which matters to employers and banks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you invest your time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Into the product, with a few customers who pay. And into learning how to talk to people who run small businesses, because I'd have to sell it myself.

say: I'd say that's enough **time** to be ready, if you start now.
I'd tell friends to stop waiting for schools to **teach** them.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with two years to build a **business** before AGI.
Robots reach the shops around **2034**, so I'd plan for that.
do: Finish the degree and take the tool to **ten shops** in the holidays.
Work with my brother Mateo on **robots** for stock and delivery.
S3.quote: Five years lets me finish my degree, build a real product and still have a plan for the robots.
fieldNote: The longer runway gets her **product-minded**: ten shops, robots, sales talk.
Degree is kept for credibility with employers and banks.
Includes her brother in her plans.

steps.text: Finish the degree for credibility with banks and employers
Take the stock tool to ten shops in the holidays
Plan robot stock handling with my brother Mateo
Put holiday earnings back into the product

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time, so don't waste it. I'd tell friends to learn, build and save. Online I'd share what I've made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be really confident. At 28 I'd have run a software business for years and know small shops better than most programmers. When AGI arrives, I'd already have customers and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish university, build the business, hire a couple of people, and keep a foot in the family shops. I'd save steadily, probably buy a small property, and give some money to the parish. I'd also look after my parents as they get older.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and fairly happy. Ten years is the sort of time where you can do a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what do you hope to have built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A software company that helps small family shops stay independent. I want to build the tools that let a small family shop survive next to the big chains. That's what I'd be proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to keep from your upbringing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The habit of working hard, the church and the sense that family comes first. Those don't change with technology, and they've kept my parents steady through bad years.

I'd tell friends to learn, build and **save**.
think: At 28 I'd have run a **software business** for years and know small shops well.
When AGI arrives I'd already have **customers** and trust.
do: Finish university, build the **business** and hire a couple of people.
Save steadily, buy a small **property** and give to the parish.
feel: **Calm** and fairly happy: a decade lets you do a lot.
S4.quote: I want to build the tools that let a small family shop survive next to the big chains.
fieldNote: Her ten-year picture is a **company** serving family shops, built on trust.
Faith, hard work and family are the constants she keeps.

steps.text: Build a software company for small family shops

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, because speed is the problem. I'd be halfway through my degree with a half-built business. What would help is clear skills training, small business support that isn't a handout, and families who can hold on together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think I'm fearless because I use AI all day. I'm not fearless, I just believe it's safer to build with the new thing than to stand in front of it.

headlineQuote: I'm not fearless, I just believe it's safer to build with the new thing than to stand in front of it.
portrait: **Chloe** is 18, studies computer science, and her parents, who own three hardware shops, pay for her room.
She uses AI every day, builds a stock tool for the shops, and sings in her parish choir.
She is calm at a plateau or a decade, and anxious when the warning is only two years.
She wants to own a business rather than hold a job, and favours skills and enterprise over handouts.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most: she'd be halfway through the degree with a half-built business.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **skills training**, small business support that isn't a handout, and families who hold together.
